The Last Lighthouse Keeper

By Mara Ellison

For forty-one years, Tomas Reyes climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the Pointe Grise lighthouse every evening at dusk. He trimmed the wick, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and kept a log every night.1 When the light was automated last spring, he was the last keeper on this stretch of coast to hand over the keys.

The keeper's cottage sits on a shelf of granite, its whitewash scoured grey by salt. Inside, the kitchen still smells of paraffin and strong coffee. Reyes, now seventy-eight, pours two cups and sits by the window that looks straight out over the reef, where the water turns from green to black in the space of a few metres.

The night shift

Most of the work, he says, was waiting. Waiting for the weather to turn, for a ship's lights to clear the headland, for the dawn. He passed the hours with a radio, a stack of paperbacks and a notebook in which he recorded the wind, the swell and anything else that caught his eye: a pod of dolphins in March, a fishing boat that lost its engine in a gale, the year the puffins did not come back.

The sea does not care whether you are watching. That is the whole point of watching it.

His routine never varied. Every evening he followed the same three steps, written on a card pinned beside the lamp room door:

  1. Clean the lens and check the mantle for cracks.
  2. Wind the rotation clock and confirm the period with a stopwatch.
  3. Record the visibility, the wind and the state of the sea.

The automation controller that replaced him runs a short configuration file. Reyes keeps a printout of it on the fridge, half as a joke and half as a reminder:

light.period = 15s
light.range_nm = 22
fog_signal.enabled = false

On clear nights he still walks up the cliff path to watch the beam sweep across the water. It is the same light, he says, but it is no longer his. Then he laughs, finishes his coffee, and asks whether we would like to see the logbooks.

  1. The logbooks are now held by the regional maritime museum. Back
